turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_process_train.csv: 300 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S, Heat treatment step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1 time, Heat treatment step 1
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2 temperature, Heat treatment step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 3 temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time, Heat treatment step 3
    cooling rate, Secondary treatment step 1 temperature, Secondary treatment step 1 time, Secondary treatment step 2
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 2 time, Secondary treatment step 3 temperature, Secondary treatment step 3
    time, Secondary treatment step 4 temperature, Secondary treatment step 4 time, Thermal exposure
    temperature, Thermal exposure time) and `target` (the measured yield strength
    at room temperature (MPa)).
  - b3_htsteel_process_pool.csv: 34 CANDIDATE samples whose yield strength
    at room temperature (MPa) was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and
    the same process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST yield
strength at room temperature (MPa), then select the 5 best candidates from
the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning from the training data

**Step 1 – Identify the candidate family.** All 34 pool entries are essentially the same alloy family: ~13 % Cr, ~0.2 % C martensitic stainless steel (410/420-type), austenitised at 1000–1050 °C and then given a single "Heat treatment step 2" tempering treatment (200–740 °C), sometimes plus an aging step. So composition differences are tiny (only Ni 0/0.6, Ti 0/0.2, Cu 0/0.3, Mn/Si 0.4–0.8) and **process — especially the tempering temperature — must do essentially all of the work.**

**Step 2 – Extract the tempering-temperature trend for 11–13 % Cr martensitics in the training set:**

| alloy | HT2 temp | YS |
|---|---|---|
| 83.7 Fe / 11.25 Cr / 0.13 C | 200 | 1330 |
| same | 400 | 1340 |
| 82.95 / 11.25 Cr | 475 | 1430 |
| same | 500 | 1190 |
| 83.7 / 11.25 Cr | 550 | 1090 |
| 82.95 / 11.25 Cr | 600 | 910 |
| 83.845 / 13 Cr / 0.4 C | 500 | 1390 |
| same, 600 (+age) | 600 | 820–840 |
| 84.125 / 13 Cr / 0.12 C | 250 | 930 |
| same | 540 | 780 |
| 84.7–84.9 / 13 Cr / 0.4 C | 530–550 | 885–960 |
| 85.3 / 13 Cr / 0.3 C | 625–650 | 700–720 |
| 84.4–84.6 / 13 Cr | 715–750 | 430–580 |
| 85.85 / 13 Cr / 0.075 C | 750 | 392 |

The trend is monotone and very strong above ~500 °C: **YS falls ~2–3 MPa per °C of tempering temperature**, from ~1300–1400 MPa for 200–500 °C tempers down to 350–580 MPa for 700–750 °C tempers. Aging at 450–600 °C after a high temper only recovers a little.

**Step 3 – Apply to the pool.** Rank essentially by Heat treatment step 2 temperature (lowest = as-quenched/low-temper martensite = strongest):

- 200 °C: c015, c021
- 300 °C: c018, c017
- 450 °C: c014, c006
- 500 °C: c004, c031
- 600 °C: c016, c027
- 715–740 °C (± aging): all the rest (c000–c013, c019–c033 subset) → predicted ~400–650 MPa, clearly the weakest.

Within the low-temper group, the 450–500 °C tempers are just as strong as 200 °C in the training analogues (peak ~1400 MPa at ~475 °C, secondary hardening), so I place those very near the top; leaner (Ni-free, Ti-free) vs. Ti/Cu-bearing variants differ negligibly.

**Predicted top group (≈1200–1450 MPa):** c015, c021, c014, c006, c031/c004, c018, c017.

## Selection

Final: c015, c021, c014, c006, c031
